claims.text: MLIPs trained on ab initio high-temperature configurations will capture the diversity of solid and liquid HEA atomic environments better than standard EAM references.
Replacing EAM references with such MLIPs will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
Improved phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
The proposed method applies to solid and ab initio liquid multicomponent HEAs, including equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, near their melting temperatures.
MLIPs such as neural-network or Gaussian-approximation potentials can be extensively trained on ab initio data spanning diverse high-temperature configurations.
At 0.9–1.0 T_m, liquid-like behavior is significant.
Compositions with five or more principal elements exhibit high configurational diversity.
An ab initio-trained MLIP potential-energy surface will faithfully interpolate across the many atomic arrangements encountered in an ab initio liquid.
Training on solid and liquid high-temperature configurations allows an MLIP to account for many-body interactions and local-environment variations that EAM potentials cannot represent.
The MLIP approach will reduce integration-path mismatch by tens of percent relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
The MLIP reference will produce more accurate thermodynamic quantities and lower statistical uncertainties.
Standard TOR-TILD EAM references have poor phase-space representation because of their limited potential form.
The intervention may provide little improvement for binary alloys or systems far from melting because their configurational diversity is low.
Inadequate coverage of high-temperature configuration space in the MLIP training data may eliminate the expected improvement.
The magnitude of mismatch reduction depends on training-set quality and range, alloy composition, and melting characteristics.

contradictions.description: The target state includes temperatures just above T_m, but the stated applicable numerical range ends at 1.0 T_m and therefore excludes temperatures above melting.

The rule associates failure with less than a 20% mismatch reduction while also requiring 'better phase-space overlap metrics'; better overlap is itself a successful outcome, making the stated decisive criterion logically ambiguous.
